summary: Source-anchored research for multikey index sort behaviour. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: When sorting on an array field indexed by a multikey index, MongoDB requires a separate sort unless every sort field has [MinKey, MaxKey] index bounds and no bounded multikey-indexed field shares a path prefix with the sort pattern. These are additional restrictions, not a replacement for ordinary compound-index sort compatibility. (high confidence)

SERVER-32525 records a historical MongoDB 3.4.10 inconsistency: filtering a.b and sorting a.c returned different orders with and without a compound multikey index. This historical example explains why predicate-bounded index order cannot automatically stand in for array sort semantics; it is not evidence of a current unfixed defect. (medium confidence)

A firsthand October 2019 report describes a sharded MongoDB 3.6.3 deployment failing an array-field descending sort with a 33554432-byte sort-memory error despite an index on transfers.amount. This is historical incident evidence, not a current memory limit or a benchmark reproduced here. (low confidence)

An IXSCAN can coexist with a blocking SORT. To assess a multikey sort, inspect the complete explain plan, including SORT, indexBounds and multiKeyPaths, rather than treating index use alone as proof that the index supplied order. Pachot demonstrates both full-bound scans without SORT and bounded scans with SORT. (high confidence)

A document sorted by an array field uses the lowest array value for ascending order and the highest for descending order. A query predicate selects documents but does not restrict sort-key selection to matching array elements. (high confidence)

Filtering custom_fields.attribute and sorting custom_fields.value is a concrete shared-prefix trap: both paths traverse custom_fields, so an equality bound on the attribute does not make the requested value sort eligible for index-provided ordering. The Candid Startup describes this application design in its July 2023 grid-view investigation. (medium confidence)

A predicate on an array does not invariably force a blocking sort: a planner can scan full array index bounds to preserve sort order and apply the predicate during FETCH. Pachot shows this candidate as a rejected alternative to a narrower IXSCAN followed by SORT; plan choice therefore involves filtering cost as well as sorting cost. (medium confidence)

If the requirement is to sort only on matched array values, MongoDB documents generating a new field with $addFields and $filter and sorting that field. This changes the sort input and should not be assumed to preserve index-provided ordering. (low confidence)

SERVER-31898 illustrates why a bounded scan can be incorrect: for find({myArray: {$gte: 5}}).sort({myArray: 1}), [1,6,7] must precede [3,4,5], although scanning only keys at least 5 encounters 5 before 6. Filtering keys can hide the actual document sort key. (high confidence)

With index {"a.b":1,"a.c":1} over an array a, filtering "a.b" while sorting "a.c" can require a separate sort even if "a.c" has full bounds. The shared prefix a lets the filter hide the element whose c value should determine document order. The Candid Startup describes the same problem for custom_fields.attribute and custom_fields.value. (high confidence)

Historical blanket advice that multikey array sorts always block is too broad for the documented behavior. The 2019 Stack Overflow answer reports no workaround, whereas SERVER-31898 records implementation of eligible nonblocking sorts with fix version 4.3.4; the manual now documents the full-bounds and path-prefix conditions. (high confidence)

Inference for compound-index design: satisfying equality-prefix and sort-direction rules does not by itself prove an array sort is index-provided. Evaluate the multikey full-bounds and shared-path restrictions separately; an index useful for filtering can still leave a separate sort. (high confidence)
